# Is Minecraft Safe for Kids? A Parents Guide & Age Rating

posted on February 25 2026

Minecraft is widely considered **kid-friendly**, especially in **single-player** or **parent-managed multiplayer**. The main safety concerns aren’t graphic content—they’re **online interactions, chat, and spending controls**.

## What is Minecraft?

Minecraft is a **sandbox video game** developed by Mojang where players build and explore worlds made of blocks. Kids can use these digital blocks to create almost anything they imagine—houses, castles, farms, or even real-world landmarks.

The game takes place in a 3D world that expands as you explore. You’ll encounter different landscapes called **biomes**, including forests, deserts, snowy mountains, and oceans. Creatures also inhabit the world—some friendly, some hostile.

Minecraft offers two main ways to play:

* **Creative Mode:** Unlimited blocks and tools so kids can focus on building with no survival danger.
* **Survival Mode:** Players gather resources, manage health and hunger, and defend themselves from hostile mobs.

Your child can play alone in **single-player** mode or connect with others in **multiplayer**. Single-player keeps the experience private and predictable. Multiplayer can be great with friends and family, but it also introduces online safety considerations.

Unlike traditional games with a fixed ending, Minecraft is open-ended. Your child decides what to do, what to build, and how to spend their time in-game.

## What Parents Need to Know about Minecraft?

### Age ratings

Minecraft is rated **PEGI 7** and **ESRB Everyone 10+**. These ratings reflect **mild fantasy violence** (combat against monsters). The game’s blocky visuals and non-graphic style make the violence less intense than many action games, but the combat is still present.

### Platform differences (Bedrock vs Java)

Minecraft comes in different editions depending on device:

**Bedrock Edition**  
 Available on Xbox, PlayStation, Nintendo Switch, mobile devices, and Windows 10/11. It supports **cross-platform play**, which makes it easy for kids to play with friends on different devices.

**Java Edition**  
 Available on PC (Windows, macOS, Linux). It’s known for a huge modding community and community-run servers, which can be amazing for creativity—but can also require extra supervision depending on what servers and mods are used.

**Legacy Console Editions**  
 Older versions on consoles like PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360. These are largely discontinued and don’t receive the same updates and safety improvements.

In general, Bedrock tends to be more consistent for families across devices, while Java offers more customization.

### Account requirements

Most versions require a **Microsoft account**. Child accounts (typically for players under 16, or under 19 in South Korea) are connected to a parent’s account. This allows parents to manage settings like multiplayer access, chat permissions, and purchase approvals.

### Combat and violence

Minecraft includes combat where players use items like swords, axes, and bows, and sometimes explosives like TNT. The violence is **stylized and non-graphic**: there’s no blood or realistic injury, and defeated characters disappear and can respawn.

## Is Minecraft Appropriate for Kids?

For many families, Minecraft is appropriate—especially with the right settings. It’s often safest when kids start in **Creative** or **single-player**, then move to supervised multiplayer when ready.

**What makes it kid-friendly:**

* Blocky, cartoon-style visuals (no realistic violence)
* No graphic gore, sexual content, or mature story themes
* Encourages creativity, spatial reasoning, and problem-solving
* Can support learning in areas like basic logic, math, and design
* Single-player mode removes online interaction risks
* Strong parental controls in modern versions

**Things to consider:**

* Mild fantasy violence (fighting hostile mobs)
* Multiplayer can expose kids to strangers and inappropriate chat
* Open-ended gameplay can make time limits harder to enforce
* Marketplace purchases may be available (especially on Bedrock)

Ultimately, it depends on your child’s maturity, whether they’ll play online, and how actively you plan to supervise. Many parents find that playing alongside their child helps them understand the game and set healthy boundaries.

## Parental controls (and how they help)

Minecraft includes tools that help parents manage online safety. Most controls are handled through Microsoft’s family settings, even if your child doesn’t play on Xbox.

Key settings you can control include multiplayer access, who can add friends, and who can message your child.

**Common controls parents use:**

* **Multiplayer access:** Allow or block online play
* **Friends list:** Manage who your child can add or interact with
* **Chat permissions:** Choose messages from everyone, friends only, or no one
* **Realms and clubs:** Control access to private servers and group features

Minecraft also includes reporting and blocking tools. Kids can report harmful behavior and mute or block other players, but these work best when paired with clear family rules and ongoing conversations about online safety.

## Benefits of Minecraft for kids

Minecraft has real upsides when used intentionally.

It supports creativity because kids can build anything from small projects to entire cities. It also strengthens problem-solving skills as children gather materials, plan builds, and adapt when things don’t work.

Multiplayer (with approved friends/family) can build social skills like teamwork, communication, and cooperation. Learning also happens naturally: kids practice reading with recipes and menus, use math when measuring or counting resources, and develop spatial skills by navigating a 3D environment.

Minecraft can also encourage planning and organization, especially in Survival Mode where resources are limited and goals require multiple steps.

## Tools and Tips for Parents

A practical approach is to start with single-player or Creative Mode so your child can learn safely. If you introduce multiplayer, consider keeping it to real-life friends or a private Realm that you control.

If your child uses the Minecraft Marketplace, enable purchase approvals and talk about spending rules early. It’s also worth explaining what griefing is (players destroying others’ builds) and how to report or block players if needed.

At JusTalk, we offer a safe and fun video calling platform for kids and families. If your child plays Minecraft with friends or wants to share builds with relatives, JusTalk supports clear 1v1 and group calls, interactive features like doodling, and encrypted messaging. [Download JusTalk Kids today](https://kids.justalk.com/download.html) to learn how JusTalk can support safer, more connected conversations.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Can my child play Minecraft completely offline?

Yes. Single-player mode works entirely offline once downloaded and your Microsoft account is authenticated. This eliminates all online risks including chat and stranger contact. You’ll need internet initially for download and occasional updates, but daily gameplay doesn’t require connectivity.

### Can siblings share one Minecraft account?

While technically possible, each child should have their own free child account linked to your parent account. This allows personalized parental controls, individual friend lists, and separate progress tracking at no extra cost. Multiple accounts can share one game purchase through console family sharing or home console settings.

### Can my child get addicted to Minecraft?

Like any engaging activity, excessive Minecraft play can become problematic. Warning signs include neglecting homework, declining physical activity, irritability when asked to stop, and loss of interest in other hobbies. Prevent issues by setting clear time limits through Microsoft Family Settings (1-2 hours daily for school days is reasonable), requiring outdoor play first, and ensuring Minecraft doesn’t replace face-to-face social interaction. The game’s creative nature makes it less addictive than reward-based games, but boundaries remain important.

# Minecraft Parental Controls: Set Them Up on Every Device

---

Minecraft’s parental controls live in your Microsoft account, not the game itself. They work in three layers: Microsoft Family Safety for screen time and purchases, Xbox privacy settings for chat and multiplayer, and your device’s own controls. Here is how to set up each one, and how to cover what they miss.

![Set up Minecraft parental controls for its 300M+ players via Microsoft Family Safety and Xbox: manage chat, multiplayer, purchases, and screen time.](minecraft.png "Parent setting up Minecraft parental controls through Microsoft Family Safety")

Minecraft looks like the safe choice. With more than 300 million copies sold, a milestone Mojang Studios confirmed in 2023, it is one of the most-played games in the world, and for many families it is the first game they say yes to without much worry. But the real risks are not in the blocks. They are in the open chat on public servers, the strangers who send friend requests, the Minecoins charges that add up, and the custom worlds nobody has vetted.

What most parents miss is that the controls that shut all of this down are not inside the game. They live in your Microsoft account, and once you set them, Minecraft follows them everywhere your child signs in.

**TL;DR**

Minecraft’s parental controls live in your Microsoft account, not the game. Set them in three free layers: Microsoft Family Safety (screen time, purchases, which games open), Xbox privacy settings (chat, multiplayer, friends), and your device’s own controls. Together they take about fifteen minutes. For limits Microsoft cannot enforce beyond Minecraft, such as YouTube, Discord, and the browser, add a device-level control on Android and Windows.

## Does Minecraft Have Parental Controls?

Yes. Because a Minecraft account is a [Microsoft account](https://www.minecraft.net/en-us/article/parental-controls), the controls live in your Microsoft settings and work in three layers that fit together:

* **Microsoft Family Safety** sets the account rules: screen time, purchases, and which games your child can open.
* **Xbox privacy and online safety settings** control multiplayer, chat, and friends, because Minecraft Bedrock Edition routes these through Xbox Live even on devices that are not an Xbox.
* **Your device or console** (Nintendo Switch, PlayStation, iPhone, or Windows) adds a second lock on time and purchases.

All three are free, and setting them up from scratch takes about fifteen minutes.

*None of the three is set inside Minecraft itself, which is why most parents never find them.*

## How to Set Up Minecraft Parental Controls

Set up the layers in order, all from a web browser. You do not need the console in front of you.

1. **Create a family group and add your child.** Following [Minecraft’s official setup guide](https://help.minecraft.net/hc/en-us/articles/4408968616077-Set-Up-Microsoft-Family-Groups-for-Parental-Controls-in-Minecraft-Bedrock-Edition), go to family.microsoft.com, sign in with your own Microsoft account, and add your child with their real birthdate. Where that age is below the age of consent for your country (13 in the United States, higher in parts of Europe), Microsoft treats the account as a child account and asks for your consent, which is what switches on the protective defaults. If your child originally signed up with a fake adult birthdate, none of those defaults apply, and you will need to create a proper child account.
2. **Lock down chat and multiplayer.** In your child’s Xbox privacy settings, set “Others can communicate with voice, text, or invites” to Block or Friends, and turn “You can join multiplayer games” off to keep your child off public servers. On a child account, Minecraft already turns multiplayer off by default, so this is mostly a matter of confirming it. Setting the privacy preset to Child switches chat and multiplayer off together.
3. **Require approval for purchases.** In your child’s spending settings, turn on “Ask a parent to buy things” so every Marketplace purchase (paid for with Minecoins) or Realms subscription needs your approval, or remove the saved payment method from the account entirely.
4. **Set a screen-time limit.** Microsoft Family Safety can cap how long Minecraft runs each day, either as a Minecraft-specific limit or as part of an overall Xbox and Windows limit.

*The order matters: a child account created with a fake birthdate leaves the next three steps with nothing to apply to.*

**Bedrock or Java? It changes what you can control**

Most versions of Minecraft, including Nintendo Switch, Xbox, PlayStation, iPhone and iPad, Windows 10 and 11, and Android, run Bedrock Edition, and the three-layer system above applies to all of them. Java Edition, which runs only on PC, has fewer built-in controls, and the main safeguard is the server your child joins. You can hide chat in-game under Settings, then Multiplayer, then Chat, but the stronger protection is sticking to known, whitelisted servers or a private Realm rather than public ones.

| Bedrock Edition | Java Edition |
| --- | --- |
| Runs on | Switch, Xbox, PlayStation, iOS, Windows 10/11, Android | PC only |
| Microsoft Family Safety and Xbox controls | Full: chat, multiplayer, purchases, screen time | Limited |
| Main safeguard | Account-level three-layer controls | The server your child joins |
| Chat control | Xbox privacy settings (Block / Friends / Child preset) | Hide chat in-game (Settings > Multiplayer > Chat) |

## What Minecraft’s Controls Can’t Do

Microsoft’s controls are strong at the account and game level, but they stop at the edge of the Microsoft world. They do not reach:

* **Player-made content and mods,** where a custom world can contain almost anything Minecraft never reviewed.
* **Discord,** where many children coordinate their Minecraft sessions and conversations move out of Minecraft’s reach.
* **YouTube and streaming,** where some children watch as much Minecraft as they play, often with unmoderated comments.
* **Java Edition’s servers,** which carry fewer built-in controls than Bedrock.

## Cover the Gaps: One Limit Across Every App

Those gaps are where a device-level control earns its place. Microsoft’s settings manage Minecraft itself well, including screen time on Windows and Xbox, but they only work while your child stays signed in to the account you set up, and they do nothing beyond it.

On Android and Windows, [Salfeld Child Control](https://salfeld.com/en/child-control/) sets time limits that cover Minecraft, YouTube, Discord and the browser, app by app or in one shared limit. Its roaming feature spreads a single daily screen time across the phone, tablet and computer instead of counting each device separately.

## Is Minecraft Safe for Kids?

By content, yes. The [ESRB rates Minecraft Everyone 10+](https://www.esrb.org/ratings/39546/minecraft/) for mild fantasy violence, [PEGI rates it 7](https://www.minecraft.net/en-us/article/parents--guide-minecraft), and [Common Sense Media](https://www.commonsensemedia.org/game-reviews/minecraft) broadly agrees. There is no drinking, drugs, or sexual content, and the fighting is bloodless. What sets Minecraft apart from a platform like [Roblox](https://salfeld.com/en/guide/kids-roblox/), where every game is built by another user, is that the blocks themselves are safe.

The danger is not the game but who your child meets while playing it. That is why the setup above targets chat, contact and spending rather than the content. Once Minecraft is locked down, our [guide to safe online games for kids](https://salfeld.com/en/guide/safe-online-games/) is worth a read for judging the next game your child asks for.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Does Minecraft have parental controls?

Yes, but they are set through your Microsoft account rather than inside the game. Microsoft Family Safety controls screen time, purchases, and which games your child can open, and Xbox privacy settings control multiplayer, chat, and friends, because Minecraft Bedrock Edition runs these through Xbox Live.

### How do I turn off chat in Minecraft?

For Bedrock Edition, open your child’s Xbox privacy settings and set “Others can communicate with voice, text, or invites” to Block, or set the profile preset to Child, which turns off chat and multiplayer together. For Java Edition, you can hide chat in-game under Settings, then Multiplayer, then Chat.

### How do I stop my child buying Minecoins?

In your child’s Microsoft Family Safety spending settings, turn on “Ask a parent to buy things” so every Marketplace or Realms purchase needs your approval, or remove the saved payment method from the account entirely.

### What age is Minecraft suitable for?

The ESRB rates Minecraft Everyone 10+ and PEGI rates it 7. The content is mild, so the deciding factor for most families is whether the child is ready for online multiplayer, which you can turn off for younger children.

### Can I set a time limit on Minecraft?

Yes. Microsoft Family Safety can set a daily limit on Minecraft specifically, or on Xbox and Windows overall. For a single limit that also covers other apps and devices, a device-level tool such as Salfeld Child Control on Android and Windows spreads one shared screen time across them.

# Minecraft Parents’ Guide

Resources and FAQs for parents of (future) Minecraft players

There’s no experience like a shared adventure with your child(ren) – and with their creativity and imagination set loose, they’ll be having many an adventure in Minecraft. If you’re a parent considering introducing your young ones to this blocky sandbox, if your child wants to play, or is already playing Minecraft, you might have questions you want answered to ensure that the game offers a safe experience.

In this article, we will run through how Minecraft **(Java Edition and Bedrock Edition)** works, how players are kept safe, parental controls available, and how to buy Minecraft. You will also find links to guides and FAQs that will strengthen your knowledge of the game.

![Steve and Alex running out of a cave.](/content/dam/minecraftnet/games/minecraft/key-art/javabedrock_boxart.jpg)

## BASICS OF MINECRAFT

Minecraft is a game made up of blocks in an ever-expanding 3D world. These blocks can be broken and [used to construct whatever you can imagine](/article/how-craft). A statue of your pet? Check! A grand castle? Definitely doable! A small hut made of dirt blocks? Perfection!

Adventure awaits around every chunk, with all sorts of different biomes (Minecraft landscapes) and creatures spread throughout the world. You can survive the night or build a work of art – there are no goals, so how you want to spend your time is up to you.

There are two different versions of Minecraft: **Java Edition** and **Bedrock Edition**. These two editions differ somewhat from each other in the sense that they are available on different platforms and offer different services. For example, in Bedrock Edition, you can access [Minecraft Marketplace](https://www.minecraft.net/marketplace) – a hub of purchasable maps, skins, and mini-games bought with the currency Minecoins, all of which are curated to ensure quality and safety.

To learn more about these two versions and which one is best suited for you, check out the guide ["The difference between Java and Bedrock Edition"](/article/java-or-bedrock-edition).

### Game modes

Minecraft can be played in both single-player (offline and alone) and multiplayer (online, with the ability to play with other players). Both Java Edition and Bedrock Edition have multiplayer turned off by default on child accounts. To enable multiplayer, read more in our [Java guide](https://help.minecraft.net/hc/en-us/articles/4410317081741) and [Bedrock guide](https://help.minecraft.net/hc/en-us/articles/4410316619533). Both modes are equally fun and it all comes down to personal preference: single-player allows you to experience the world at your own pace, and multiplayer is a great way to connect with both family and friends through couch co-op and distant play.

There are also [two different play modes](/article/creative-vs-survival-mode): **Creative mode**, which focuses on the building aspects of Minecraft, and **Survival mode**, which puts emphasis on survival with mechanics such as hunger and health.

### Age rating

The game has a recommended PEGI rating of 7 and an ESRB rating of Everyone 10+. However, Minecraft has players of all ages, and if you play with your child, you might find yourself enthralled by Minecraft's blocky charm.

![Steve and Alex running through a colorful landscape together with a bunch of mobs.](/content/dam/minecraftnet/games/minecraft/key-art/pi-2.jpg)

## IS MINECRAFT SAFE?

We believe that Minecraft should be a safe space for everyone, regardless of whether you’re playing alone in single-player, or together with others in multiplayer. We work actively to improve online safety for all our players no matter their age.

One of the best things about Minecraft is the amazing community and the people you’ll meet in multiplayer modes. There’s nothing better than getting together with like-minded players to collaborate on amazing builds, play together on Realms, or compete on multiplayer servers.

### Resources

We understand it can be scary having your child interact with unknown people, so to make sure they have the best and safest experience possible, we have several resources and tools that you can utilize to tailor your child’s multiplayer experience.

* **[Parental controls](https://www.minecraft.net/article/parental-controls)**  
   A guide to control tools available to parents within Minecraft.
* **[How to stay safe online](https://www.minecraft.net/article/minecraft-multiplayer-server-safety)**  
   A collection of online safety tips when playing Minecraft on multiplayer
* **[Our commitment to player safety](https://help.minecraft.net/hc/en-us/articles/8047895358605)**  
   Explains in detail Mojang Studios' mission and dedication to creating the safest player experience possible
* **[How to manage parental consent, family settings, and multiplayer access for child accounts](https://help.minecraft.net/hc/en-us/articles/4408968616077)**  
   A walkthrough of the many features and settings available for child security in Minecraft
* **[Understanding Minecraft Social Features for Child Safety Online](https://help.minecraft.net/hc/en-us/articles/360058605852)**  
   An outline of the different ways players can message each other through the game, or through other messaging systems

![Steve and Alex fighting a snowman with bow and sword.](/content/dam/minecraftnet/games/minecraft/key-art/pi-3.jpg)

### Violence

There’s an aspect of combat in Minecraft’s gameplay. Because combat is part of the game, there are some elements of mild violence. Players can hit and defeat (essentially, kill) both passive and hostile creatures (also known as ‘mobs’), as well as other players (if playing in multiplayer mode). There's also some use of weapons, such as swords, axes, bows, and TNT.

However, the visual representation of the violence is limited by Minecraft’s simple and cartoony style. There’s no blood in any part of the game, neither coming from creatures nor the environment. Players can’t die permanently and will respawn if their health reaches zero (unless they’re playing on Hardcore mode, a sub-genre of Survival mode).

### Griefing

When it comes to unwanted player violence like 'griefing' (a deliberate act that hurts the progress of other players and goes against the rules of the game), we encourage players to [report griefing behavior](https://help.minecraft.net/hc/en-us/articles/4409161646989-Player-and-Server-Griefing-Issues-FAQ). Please note that the act of griefing only can occur in multiplayer – *not* single-player.

![Steve and Alex armed with weapons, together with a pig on an isolated background.](/content/dam/minecraftnet/games/minecraft/key-art/pi-1.jpg)

## HOW DO I BUY MINECRAFT?

Getting Minecraft is easy! All you need to do is head over to the page [Get Minecraft](https://www.minecraft.net/store/minecraft-deluxe-collection-pc). There, you can learn more about pricing, as well as which edition you will need for your specific platform of choice.

### Accounts for parents and children

To set up Minecraft for your child(ren), you will need a minimum of two accounts, including a "**child account**". A child account is an account for those under the age of 16 for the US & EU, and 19 for South Korea, and cannot exist without an adult Microsoft account tied to it. The adult must use an existing adult Microsoft account, or they can create a new adult Microsoft account that will then become the organizer and manager for the child account. Only adult accounts can modify family settings for children, like enabling multiplayer settings.

To learn how to set up an account, check out our guide [How to create a Minecraft account](https://www.minecraft.net/article/how-create-minecraft-account).

To set or edit parental controls for your child’s account, visit <http://account.xbox.com/settings> and then click the account that you want to edit. You should see your child’s gamertag in the top right.

# Is Minecraft Safe for Kids? Age Rating: Parents Guide to Safety

![](https://funtechsummercamps.com/blog/wp-content/uploads/2020/01/minecraft-for-parents.jpg)

Minecraft is the highest selling video game of all time. Almost a decade after its first release it continues to be one of the most popular games, particularly among children. But many parents have little to no understanding of what the game involves, what the Minecraft age rating is, what dangers could come with it and how long they should let their kids play it for. Some parents even question whether Minecraft is safe for kids.

At FunTech we understand the power Minecraft has to educate and support children’s learning development. We’ve even previously blogged about [how Minecraft can set a child up for life](https://funtechsummercamps.com/blog/minecraft-coding-for-kids-how-it-can-set-your-child-up-for-life/) in terms of a career, and listed [11 reasons why we believe it has educational value](https://funtechsummercamps.com/blog/11-reasons-why-minecraft-is-educational-for-kids/).

In fact, we even run summer camps dedicated to teaching children how to code using the Minecraft video game ([view all camp dates here](https://funtechsummercamps.com/course-descriptions)).

## Minecraft age rating

**According to the official website, the current Minecraft age rating is recommended PEGI 7 and an ESRB rating of Everyone 10+.**

But we still appreciate that Minecraft can be a tricky subject to navigate given the concerns over screen time and online risks. With that in mind, we wanted to put this guide together which explains what parents need to know about Minecraft.

## Minecraft parent’s guide (is Minecraft good for kids)

Minecraft is regarded as one of the most influential games of all time, with millions of players, spin-off games and even an annual convention. But, in a world where video games are part and parcel with everyday life, how can you be sure that your child is safe playing Minecraft?

This informative guide will lay out all you need to know about the video game so you can be confident that you know exactly what your child is doing online and that they are safe and having fun either on their own or with online friends.

### What is Minecraft about?

While most video games have some kind of plot or even an objective, such as rescuing a princess in Mario, defeating the ‘bad guys’, or even running a farm in more peaceful games such as Stardew Valley, Minecraft is unique in the fact that it doesn’t have a plot.

Rather than giving the player any kind of prompt, such as ‘go to this location’ or ‘find this’, the game gives no instructions at all and instead allows you to figure out what you want to do in its world.

Known as a ‘sandbox game’, Minecraft allows for the complete creative freedom of the player. The entire world of Minecraft is comprised entirely of 1×1 3D blocks, including grass blocks that make up the ground, trunk blocks that are stacked up to form trees and even water blocks that flow into rivers and oceans.

These blocks can be broken and picked up by the player, who can then re-place them around the world to build houses, castles or other structures. This is where the ‘mining’ aspect comes from, including literally mining for iron, gold and coal.

### What do kids do in Minecraft?

There is no story or objective in Minecraft. Kids are left entirely to their own devices. Whether you choose to create a small homestead to farm and trade with villagers (computer-controlled characters that inhabit the world) or build the biggest structure you can.

The game is itself a survival experience, with your character having a basic health bar that can take damage from falling, being attacked by randomly generated enemies or even by forgetting to eat.

You keep your health bar up by being aware of your surroundings, eating food (including apples from trees, vegetables you’ve farmed from seeds, food you have crafted from wheat or even meat from the animals you come across in the environment).

Typically, the choices made by players is between creative and survival. Some kids choose to ignore the survival elements of the game (which can be controlled through the game settings, such as turning off enemies and the health bar) and simply use the game in order to build stuff.

You may have seen images online of gigantic structures created in the game, such as recreations of famous sights or fictional settings, or even designs purely from the imagination of the builder.

However, other kids choose to focus on the survival elements of the game. This is usually the route chosen by most players starting out, using the materials found in the area they are put into to build a shelter before the first night falls.

The official Minecraft website has a useful ‘[How To](https://www.minecraft.net/en-us/article/how-minecraft)’ guide to starting out a game in Minecraft for beginners.

### What age rating is appropriate for Minecraft?

Minecraft age rating by most parents we’ve spoken to is typically for ages 8 and up, being a game that isn’t overly violent or even that difficult to learn how to use. In fact, for many children, it was one of their first video game experiences online.

Some parents have asked us whether Minecraft suitable for 6 year olds. Whilst many parents will let their kids play from 6 years of age and it is fun for most ages, we do recommend you follow the guidelines set out by the developers and online safety advisors many of whom say Minecraft is ok for a 7 year old as an age rating.

While you are not asked for proof of age when you are setting up an account, you are asked for your birthday when setting up an account. If the game registers that you are under 13 then certain elements are locked, including making in-game purchases.

However, it is very easy for a child to be aware of these restrictions and choose to enter a birth year that allows them full access to all the features.

There are certain settings that can be controlled in order to create an experience that you are comfortable for your child to have, including changing the difficulty to stop monsters from generating in the world and even turning off the health bar that prevents you from dying.

### Is Minecraft safe for kids?

Minecraft is generally safe for kids as it’s purposefully child-friendly in both is visual design and its gameplay, with even the monsters being cuter than actually scary. But as with any video games and online activity, there are caveats with this.

Allowing your child to play video games unsupervised is something many parents worry about, especially if you are unfamiliar with the game. This is understandable, with game ratings on the boxes not being specific about how violent the game is.

The combat within the game is very simple, with damage being taken off of your health bar if you are hit by a monster or their weapon (and vice versa if you are attacking a monster). If you choose to fight, hearts appear around the monster to show damage is being taken instead of any visible injuries or blood.

The only truly ‘scary’ element to the game could arguably be the night-time and the audio of unseen monsters (with zombies making stereotypical moans and skeletons rattling), but this can easily be fixed by turning the audio of the monsters down in the settings.

Ultimately, every child has different limits and find different things challenging or scary. While Minecraft is not really considered to be scary or overly violent, you still know your child’s limits better than anyone and should be able to make an educated guess as to whether your child would find Minecraft too scary or challenging.

If you are still unsure, either try playing Minecraft for yourself or be with your child when they are first starting out to see how they react to the game.

### Does Minecraft cost anything?

As with most video games, you have to buy Minecraft in order to play it. One of the great things about Minecraft is that it is cross-platform, meaning that it is available to play both on your home computer and on game consoles, phones, tablets and even on your Amazon Fire TV.

You will get the choice of what platform you want to play Minecraft on, which will then lead you to the specific purchase screen for that version of Minecraft.

The price of Minecraft depends on the platform you are purchasing it on, with some costing more than others and certain platforms having more than one version available.

The base game is essentially the same in most editions, with certain elements being different depending on the system.

### Are there any additional costs to Minecraft?

Once you have bought Minecraft you can then play the game without any compulsory additional spend, such as any kind of subscription fees or hidden costs. However, there are certain additional features that can be purchased.

* **Texture and skin packs:** Texture packs are buyable ‘packs’ that change the look of your Minecraft blocks, with the literal textures of the world being changed to be brighter, darker or even different colours. There are hundreds of texture packs online, with some being available for free for platforms such as home computer, while others are buyable from Minecraft. Skin packs are the same, only they change the appearance of your character.
* **Minecraft Realms:** Minecraft Realms is an online membership for Minecraft that allows you to operate your own multiplayer servers. While basic Minecraft allows for only one player per world, Realms allows for multiple players to play within the same game no matter where they are in the world. These realms are completely controllable by you, allowing you to change the difficulty and the look and feel of the game.
* **Online Multiplayer:** For certain consoles such as Nintendo Switch, online multiplayer is only available to those who have an online membership. This doesn’t apply to all versions of Minecraft.

### Is Minecraft violent?

Video game violence is a common worry for parents, and while it hasn’t been proven to be a direct cause of real-life violence there are still certain things that you may be concern about what your child sees and takes part in when they are gaming.

Certain video games such as Doom and other popular shoot-em-ups can involve a lot of blood and violence that could disturb children of a certain age.

However, while Minecraft does have certain elements of light violence it is extremely mild and cartoonish in its style. The monsters that appear are easily defeated via swords and bows and arrows, disappearing in a puff of smoke once ‘killed’, with the only hints towards blood being the red hearts that come off of them when they are hit.

The level of violence in Minecraft is optional and easily changed in the settings, with the level of difficulty dictating how many monsters generate into the world, if at all.

If you do not want any monsters or enemies appearing in your game, simply set the difficulty to ‘Peaceful’.

However, even without monsters, there are still ways to kill in the game. Swinging swords at non-playable characters such as villagers and traders can kill them (although for no reward), and animals such as sheep and chickens can be attacked for meat, wool and feathers which make important crafting tools (although sheers can be crafted to harvest wool later on).

You don’t have to kill anything in the game, however, as meat isn’t a necessary resource to regain health as there is plenty of alternative foods such as carrots, bread and potatoes for your character to cook and eat.

### Can Minecraft make you smarter?

Minecraft is often lauded as being incredibly educational, but is that actually true and can Minecraft make you smarter?

Because of its range of elements including survival mode and creative mode, you can tailor the experience of your game to make it more problem solving or creative.

We’ve previously blogged about [the educational aspects of Minecraft](https://funtechsummercamps.com/blog/11-reasons-why-minecraft-is-educational-for-kids/), and here are our points in short:

1. It can help kids learn problem solving techniques.
2. It can support reading and writing skills.
3. It supports a curious mind.
4. It helps kids with maths problems.
5. It teaches kids how to manage resources.
6. It teaches kids the benefits of teamwork.
7. It can help improve a child’s confidence.
8. It can help kids learn about history.
9. It can improve a child’s creativity and imagination.
10. It can help a child learn how to code.
11. It offers valuable future work skills.

One of the great things about Minecraft is that over the years since its launch it has become far more complex than just stacking blocks.

The material ‘redstone’ powers a range of different pistons and rail tracks, allowing for fully automated circuitry to be built (you may have seen articles about players creating fully working hard drives within their Minecraft servers).

### Is there online chat in Minecraft?

While the base Minecraft game is usually a single-player game, it does have multiplayer. This can be local (as in, playing alongside a nearby computer or console) or far-reaching (with players from all over the world being able to play simultaneously).

When joining a multiplayer server, Minecraft will display a disclaimer telling your child that they may be exposed to open chatrooms that have not been rated (and therefore contain language or content suitable for all ages). Through Minecraft itself players can only communicate through a text chat, other applications such as Skype or Discord can allow your child to audibly talk with friends.

Multiplayer is the only way someone can talk to your child through Minecraft is to join a multiplayer server, so you shouldn’t be concerned for their safety if they are playing a solo game.

The official Minecraft website has a [useful guide to online safety](https://www.minecraft.net/en-us/article/minecraft-multiplayer-server-safety) when using Minecraft, which you should check out if you are still unsure about whether to allow your child to play on multiplayer servers.

### How long should your child play Minecraft for?

While spending time online or playing games isn’t necessarily a bad thing, parents should be aware of how long their child is spending online compared to spending time outside or even just engaging in something that is not on a screen (such as a book, a board game or fighting with their siblings).

Minecraft is an incredibly engrossing game, being incredibly easy to sink hours upon hours at a time in. Time flies when you are having fun and before you know it you have spent the last four hours building the perfect Minecraft block house without intending to.

Some professionals recommend certain lengths of time for children to spend on screens, recommending children 12 and younger should only have a maximum of 2 hours per day.

However, this is easier said than done in today’s digital world, and your child may find it hard to not engage in something that their friends spend all their time on too. In that case, it may well be that you tailor the amount of time around your own child.

Too much of anything is bad, so keep an eye on how long your child is spending per day on video games compared to other activities. Make sure that they are taking part in enough non-screen activities, such as taking them out for walks during downtime, encouraging them to take part in extra-curricular activities in and out of school (such as football, dancing or more creative activities like art or music lessons).

### What can you build in Minecraft?

The possibilities of what you can build in Minecraft is literally endless, and even though building things out of 1×1 cubes may make it seem like you could only build a very square house, adults and children have managed to create incredibly complex and sometimes fully operational structures.

If you are still stuck for ideas of what to build, there are also entire websites dedicated to sharing blueprints and images of other people’s Minecraft creations that are relatively simple to build.

Whether you want to build a realistic looking ancient oak tree to complete your garden, a car to put in your garage or even recreating your favourite character in block-form.

[Grabcraft.com](https://www.grabcraft.com/) has hundreds of free-to-use blueprints, from buildings and statues to characters and even working machines.

# Is Minecraft Safe for Kids?

Minecraft is rated E10+ by the ESRB and 9+ in Apple’s App Store, and it’s one of the gentler popular games: no blood, blocky fights, and online play switched off by default on child accounts. The risks sit in the online parts, such as servers, chat and in-game purchases, and each one has a setting you control.

By **the CITA Editorial Team**Updated October 5, 20267 min read

Here’s what the ratings mean, what fits each age, and how to set Minecraft up for your child in about 15 minutes.

Fast Facts About Minecraft Safety

* The ESRB rates Minecraft E10+ for Fantasy Violence, and adds Users Interact and In-Game Purchases.[[1]](#sources)
* There’s no blood anywhere in the game, and players who lose all their health simply respawn.[[2]](#sources)
* Multiplayer is off by default on child accounts in both Java Edition and Bedrock Edition.[[2]](#sources)
* In the US and EU, Minecraft treats every account for someone under 16 as a child account that a parent manages.[[4]](#sources)
* Parental controls don’t work on Minecraft versions older than 1.16.4 or on modded versions.[[4]](#sources)

If your child is in danger right now

* Call 911 if there is an immediate threat.
* Report exploitation to the NCMEC CyberTipline: [report.cybertip.org](https://report.cybertip.org/) or 1-800-843-5678.
* If sexual images of your child are being shared or threatened, [Take It Down](https://takeitdown.ncmec.org/) can help remove them.
* If your child is thinking about suicide, call or text 988.

## What Age Is Minecraft For?

Minecraft’s ratings put it at roughly 7 to 10 and up, depending on who is rating it. Minecraft’s own parents’ guide notes that the game has players of all ages.[[2]](#sources)

| Rating | Minecraft’s rating | What it tells you |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ESRB (US and Canada) | E10+: Fantasy Violence. Also Users Interact and In-Game Purchases.[[1]](#sources) | Generally suitable for ages 10 and up.[[5]](#sources) |
| PEGI (Europe) | PEGI 7[[2]](#sources) | Europe’s rating board places it lower than the ESRB does. |
| Apple App Store (US) | 9+[[3]](#sources) | Lists infrequent cartoon or fantasy violence, messaging and chat, and user-generated content.[[3]](#sources) |

The ESRB’s E10+ rating describes the game itself. Its Users Interact label warns that once your child plays online, they may run into unfiltered content and messages from other players.[[1]](#sources)[[5]](#sources)

### A Practical Age Guide

* **Under 7:** Single-player Creative mode, on a screen you can see. Leave multiplayer off.
* **7 to 9:** Single-player, plus playing with people they know in real life, such as siblings on the same network or friends you invite to a private world. Keep chat limited to friends.
* **10 to 12:** This is the age the ESRB rating fits. If you turn on multiplayer, keep communication to friends and talk about what to do when a stranger messages them.
* **13 and older:** Teens often want public servers, where they’ll meet people they don’t know. Agree on the rules together, and keep purchases behind your approval.

For children 5 to 10, the American Academy of Pediatrics suggests playing video games together to see whether you like the messages and behavior they show, and notes that parental controls help but aren’t 100% effective.[[6]](#sources)

## What’s Actually in the Game

Minecraft is a building and survival game made of blocks. Kids gather materials, build anything they can imagine, and in Survival mode defend themselves against monsters. In Creative mode there’s no survival pressure at all, just building.[[2]](#sources)

* **Violence is mild and cartoonish.** Players fight monsters such as zombies and skeletons with swords, axes and bows. They can also hurt animals and villagers, though the game doesn’t encourage it.[[1]](#sources)
* **There’s no blood,** and players don’t die permanently in standard play. They respawn when their health runs out.[[2]](#sources)
* **There are two versions:** Bedrock Edition, which includes the Minecraft Marketplace, and Java Edition.[[2]](#sources) Bedrock runs on consoles, phones, tablets and Windows, and Java runs on computers.

## Where the Real Risks Are

### Strangers on Servers

Multiplayer servers are online worlds where your child can play with people they’ve never met, and many are run by other players or companies, not by Minecraft’s makers. Chat on those servers is where most of the risk lives. Both versions let players block, mute or report someone from the pause menu, and Java Edition has a Player Reporting tool that sends abusive chat to Minecraft’s moderators, including from private servers.[[4]](#sources)[[7]](#sources)

Watch for the same warning signs as any game: a new online friend who gives gifts or attention, asks to keep things secret, or wants to move the conversation to another app. Our guide to the [signs of online grooming](/online-safety/grooming/) explains what that looks like.

### Spending

Bedrock Edition’s Marketplace sells maps, skins and mini-games for Minecoins, an in-game currency bought with real money. Minecraft says Marketplace content is curated for quality and safety.[[2]](#sources) The App Store also lists Realms subscriptions, which host a private world for invited friends.[[3]](#sources) Purchase approvals are covered in the settings below.

### Mods and Downloads

Mods, maps and add-ons from outside the official Marketplace are popular, especially for Java Edition. Minecraft doesn’t provide parental controls for modded versions of the game.[[4]](#sources) Ask to see a download before it’s installed, and stick to sites you’ve looked at together.

### Hours That Keep Growing

Minecraft has no end, which is part of its appeal and part of why stopping is hard. The World Health Organization defines gaming disorder as impaired control over gaming, gaming taking priority over other interests, and continuing despite harm, usually for at least 12 months. It notes that only a small proportion of players develop it.[[8]](#sources) If you’re worried, our [video game addiction test](/video-game-addiction-test/?take=1) takes a few minutes.

## Minecraft Parental Controls, Step by Step

Minecraft’s controls live in your child’s Microsoft account, not inside the game. Bedrock Edition, Java Edition and Realms all require a Microsoft account, even if your child doesn’t play on an Xbox.[[4]](#sources)

1. **Set up a child account under your own account.** Only a parent account can change the settings. If your child already has an account, create your own Microsoft account and link theirs to it.[[4]](#sources)
2. **Go to account.xbox.com/settings** and choose your child’s account.[[4]](#sources)
3. **Decide on multiplayer.** Under Online Safety, “You can join multiplayer games” controls online play, and “You can create and join clubs” covers clubs and Realms.[[4]](#sources) Multiplayer starts off for child accounts.[[2]](#sources)
4. **Decide on friends.** Also under Online Safety, “You can add friends on Xbox Live” controls whether your child can add new friends.[[4]](#sources)
5. **Limit who can talk to them.** Under Privacy, “Others can communicate with voice, text, or invites” can be set to Everyone, Friends or Block. Friends is a sensible default.[[4]](#sources)
6. **Set screen time and purchase limits** in the Xbox Family Settings app or at account.microsoft.com/family. Those settings also cover content filters and online purchases.[[9]](#sources)
7. **Keep the game updated.** Safety features started in version 1.16.4 and have grown since, so older versions miss them.[[4]](#sources)

If your child plays on a Nintendo Switch, a PlayStation or a Chromebook, set that platform’s own parental controls too.[[4]](#sources) Our guide to [safe video games by age](/online-safety/video-games-by-age/) lists what each console’s controls can do.

## Is Minecraft Adding Age Verification?

Microsoft, which owns Minecraft, has started asking some account holders to verify their age. Its age assurance FAQ says users in the United Kingdom, Australia, Brazil and Singapore can verify now, with a selfie-based age estimate, an ID document or a government login.[[10]](#sources)

* Adults who don’t verify can’t buy or download games and apps rated 18+. Games already owned stay playable.[[10]](#sources)
* Microsoft says the checks are handled by its partners Yoti and Verifymy, and the information is deleted once the check is complete.[[10]](#sources)
* The FAQ doesn’t list the United States as of October 2026.[[10]](#sources)

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What age is Minecraft appropriate for?

The ESRB rates Minecraft E10+, PEGI rates it 7, and the App Store lists it at 9+.[[1]](#sources)[[2]](#sources)[[3]](#sources) Many younger children play single-player Creative mode with a parent nearby. Online play is where age matters most.

### Is Minecraft safe for a 6-year-old?

Single-player Minecraft is generally gentle: no blood, blocky combat, and a Creative mode built around building rather than survival.[[2]](#sources) For a child that young, keep multiplayer off, which is the default on a child account, and play together when you can.[[2]](#sources)

### Can kids talk to strangers on Minecraft?

Only if multiplayer and communication are turned on. On a child account, multiplayer starts off, and you choose whether others can communicate with your child: everyone, friends only, or no one.[[2]](#sources)[[4]](#sources)

### Does Minecraft have in-game purchases?

Yes. Bedrock Edition’s Marketplace sells maps, skins and mini-games for Minecoins, which are bought with real money, and Realms is a paid subscription.[[2]](#sources)[[3]](#sources) Set purchase approvals in your family settings.[[9]](#sources)

### Is Planet Minecraft safe?

Planet Minecraft is a third-party community site, not part of Minecraft. Minecraft doesn’t provide parental controls for modded versions of the game.[[4]](#sources) If your child wants to download something, look at it together first.

### Do parental controls work on Java Edition?

Yes. Java Edition uses the same Microsoft account settings for multiplayer and communication, and adds a Player Reporting tool for abusive chat.[[4]](#sources)

## What Parental Controls Can Do For You

Setting parental controls on your family’s game consoles and other devices helps you manage your child’s video game use, even when you’re not around. You can easily block games by rating, control spending, limit the time your children play, and restrict online communication.

![Setting parental controls will help you manage your children’s video game use. ESRB.](/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Parental-Controls-video_thumbnail2-1024x576.jpg)

## Frequently Asked Questions

Setting parental controls on your devices will help you manage your children’s video game use, even when you’re not around.

[Do all devices have parental controls?](#do-all-devices-have-parental-controls)

Virtually every device that plays video games (consoles, PCs, smartphones, etc.) include parental controls to help you manage your kids’ video game experiences.

[What is the most important first step when I’m looking to set parental controls?](#what-is-the-most-important-first-step-when-im-looking-to-set-parental-controls)

Setting up child accounts for each of your children. Every device allows you to create child accounts for your kids, and it is a very important step of the process. Child accounts automatically provide guardrails against the collection of some data and allow you to set parental controls. In some cases, child accounts also automatically put some settings into effect. For example, Fortnite’s Cabined Accounts automatically block voice chat and real-money purchases until you provide consent. If you have several kids using one console, different accounts also help make sure a younger child doesn’t accidentally get exposed to a game or service that you’ve deemed appropriate for your older child (or for you!). Make sure you always put in your children’s correct birthdates when setting up their accounts and pick a password or PIN that only you know. These steps will help you continue to manage your kid’s video game use and provide flexibility as they grow and mature.

[Can I set parental controls to manage my kids’ screen time?](#can-i-set-parental-controls-to-manage-my-kids-screen-time)

Yes, virtually all modern devices offer the ability to manage screen time in some capacity. Some devices allow you to simply set an amount of daily game time, while many offer the ability to set weekly schedules for when your kids can play and for how long. Regardless, the device will simply shut off once your kids hit the allotted amount of time.

[Can parental controls be set to make sure my kids don’t play something potentially inappropriate?](#can-parental-controls-be-set-to-make-sure-my-kids-dont-play-something-potentially-inappropriate)

Yes, you can block access to games based on the ESRB-assigned rating information. Some devices, like the PlayStation 5, go by the age of the child. For example, if your child is 12, games rated T for Teen, M for Mature 17+, and AO for Adults Only 18+ will be blocked. Other devices let you block based on the specific age rating. Either way, you always have the ability to make exceptions and allow more restrictively rated games if you decide it’s appropriate for your family.

[Can I make sure my kids don’t play with strangers online?](#can-i-make-sure-my-kids-dont-play-with-strangers-online)

Yes, all devices include settings to manage with whom kids can play online. On some consoles you can block communication entirely. Meanwhile, others allow you to curate friends lists to make sure your kids are only playing with people they know in real life.

[How can I make sure my kids don’t spend money on new games or in-game purchases?](#how-can-i-make-sure-my-kids-dont-spend-money-on-new-games-or-in-game-purchases)

All devices have settings to help you limit or block spending money on in-game purchases or new games. Some devices can even be set to provide your kids with an allowance so they can decide how they want to spend money in a controlled environment.

[Are there other tips for managing my kids’ video game experiences?](#are-there-other-tips-for-managing-my-kids-video-game-experiences)

Visit ESRB’s Family Gaming Guide for conversation starters that will help you set household rules around video games. The Family Gaming Guide has helpful tips for managing screen time, preserving your child’s privacy, picking appropriate games, and more!
